title: Recovery sleep after sleep deprivation
description: In animals, adenosine builds up in the brain the longer they stay awake and is one of the signals behind sleepiness; in humans this has not yet been shown directly. Adenosine acts through receptors such as the A1 adenosine receptor. One study measured how many of these receptors were available in men kept awake for 52 hours, and again after 14 hours of recovery sleep. Staying awake raised receptor availability; recovery sleep brought it back to the level of well-rested people. In this episode brightness stands for A1 receptor availability, not activity. In the first part it shows the difference from well-rested people; in "What changed" it shows the change after recovery sleep.
caveat: All findings come from one PET study of 14 healthy young men after 52 hours awake, which is far longer than a usual night without sleep; the well-rested comparison came from a separate earlier group. "Frontal cortex" is drawn on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, "occipital" on the visual cortex and "parietal" on the inferior parietal cortex, which are approximations. The anterior cingulate is drawn on its dorsal part and the temporal cortex on the lateral temporal cortex, also approximations. The striatum is drawn as the caudate and putamen. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: After 52 hours awake, A1 adenosine receptor availability is higher than in well-rested people, significantly so in the frontal, occipital and parietal cortex.

phases.name: 14 hours of recovery sleep
phases.caption: A long recovery sleep of 14 hours. The brain is drawn at rest here.

citations.authors: Elmenhorst D, Elmenhorst EM, Hennecke E, Kroll T, Matusch A, Aeschbach D, Bauer A
citations.title: Recovery sleep after extended wakefulness restores elevated A<sub>1</sub> adenosine receptor availability in the human brain.
citations.quote: F]CPFPX positron emission tomography was used to quantify A1AR availability in 15 healthy male adults after 52 h of sleep deprivation and following 14 h of recovery sleep.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: After recovery sleep, receptor availability is lower than it was after staying awake, in every region measured: most in the striatum and thalamus, by about 14%, and least in the insula and temporal cortex, by about 10 to 11%.

citations.authors: Elmenhorst D, Elmenhorst EM, Hennecke E, Kroll T, Matusch A, Aeschbach D, Bauer A
citations.title: Recovery sleep after extended wakefulness restores elevated A<sub>1</sub> adenosine receptor availability in the human brain.
citations.quote: F]CPFPX positron emission tomography was used to quantify A1AR availability in 15 healthy male adults after 52 h of sleep deprivation and following 14 h of recovery sleep.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: After recovery sleep, receptor availability no longer differed from well-rested people. People whose receptor availability fell more with recovery sleep had coped better with the sleep loss, which the authors found counterintuitive.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Part of the striatum, where receptor availability fell most after recovery sleep, by about 14%, in one study.
